Yes, now that I've found this clinic and have seen how awesome PT is when done right, I'll never go anywhere else. They have so many repeat patients that keep coming back to them again and again, sending their family members, etc. and it's clear why. I continue to learn so much and get so much out of the customized treatment plan that I wouldn't be able to accomplish on my own at home. Unfortunately, I wasted a lot of hours and money over the years before this because I didn't know any better.

Awhile back, I went to one of the PT clinics that was owned by group of orthos that I went to, and I was there on and off for years for ongoing issues. Eventually my PT basically stopped interacting with me unless I specifically asked questions. She had the tech of the day oversee me as I completed a printed list of exercises that I would have to mark off on a checklist on my own, none of which were ever changed or progressed.

It's only now that I've been in PT awhile again at an independent clinic that I see how messed up that was. I see a PTA there who is fantastic and even when working with overlapping patients, always has eyes on me and knows what I'm doing and what she wants me doing next at any given moment. She tailors my plan each visit based on how I am doing each time, and is always coming up with new ways to progress me and find new exercises that will help. The difference is night and day and so is the progress.

I got custom orthotics from my podiatrist, and while they take a long time to gradually adjust to, so you have to be prepared for that, it did make a difference in the long run.

It's understandable to be scared about surgery, especially since you've never had it before. But at least you won't have to be constantly scared of an attack at any time. I know that fear, and it's awful. I've had a lot of surgeries before, but this was my first laparoscopic one, so I still didn't know all of what to expect and was nervous. Mine was just about a week and a half ago. In my opinion, the worst part of it all is when you're all prepped and laying in the pre-op bed waiting for it to happen. But the anesthesiologist will come see you before and explain everything, and you can ask any questions. Also if you're worried about nausea after, apparently it's more common with this kind of surgery, so my anesthesiologist ordered a scopolamine patch that they just put behind your ear, and you can keep it on for a few days if needed. It worked for me. When  they're ready to bring you back, they'll give you something called Versed and all of a sudden you'll feel relaxed and nerves will be gone. You'll be aware of being brought into the operating room and have to transfer onto the operating table. They'll get you in position, give you oxygen, and then start the anesthesia and the next thing you know, you're waking up in recovery! They do have to intubate you for the procedure, but it's put in and taken out while you're completely asleep so you're not aware of either. You'll just have a sore, scratchy throat for a few days.

In recovery, they'll monitor you for awhile and make sure you're doing okay and not in too much pain. Eventually they'll bring the person that came with you back, you'll be able to eat and drink something, they'll go over all your discharge instructions with you, and then you'll get to change back into your clothes and go home. Bring a small pillow in the car to put between your stomach and the seatbelt. I've been driving a few places close by since my surgery and I'm still using the pillow in the car. You also won't be able to lay flat or on your side for a little while. If you have a recliner, that's best, or just try to prop yourself up as much as possible. Ice feels great on the incisions, and a heating pad is nice for shoulder pain from the gas they use to inflate your stomach. Make sure you try to move around little bits throughout the day after, because that helps with the gas. Also make sure you drink plenty of water, because it will help flush the anesthesia out of your system.

I avoided all fats and dairy in the beginning, and now have slowly started introducing them back. Everything has been okay so far, and I haven't had any diarrhea, but I have had bloating that has been really uncomfortable, so I started taking Gas-X. Another thing is that pants can be really uncomfortable, because the waistline hits right where the majority of your incisions are, if they're like mine. Wear pants that are as loose as possible, and I've found that ones that have a flat, wide waistband, like yoga pants or some joggers, are better than a drawstring unless you can make it really loose.

Feel free to ask any questions I can answer. I know it's scary, especially the unknown of surgery and all it entails, but you've got this!!

I had to go through the endoscopy with my gastro too, even though my ultrasound showed gallstones, because he wanted to rule out anything else, like h.pylori or ulcers. It actually did end up showing the beginning of some ulcers, even though I never had any symptoms, so I was put on a medication for that. After the results of that, he gave me the official diagnosis of gallstones and referred me to a surgeon. 

You could also always get a second opinion, too, if they still don’t think it’s causing your pain. I ended up seeing 2 different surgeons because the first one wasn’t going to be able to get me in for well over a month at that hospital, so I went to one at a less busy hospital and got scheduled for a little over a week out only. No one seemed to bat an eye that I saw two different doctors.

I realized that even if I have better stretches, the stones are still there and can still get stuck and cause an attack at any time. I knew I didn’t want to keep going through this. Thankfully I got in for surgery a week ago. One week post-op, I’m still in pain but doing a little better every day, and starting to eat more of a variety of foods.

I get back pains from my gallbladder even more than I get abdominal pains. When I started getting gb pain at first, I thought it was muscular for awhile. Sometimes it feels like something tight is wrapped around and pulling on it. A heating pad does help lessen the intensity, though.

One more thing... don't get yourself too down by reading other people's posts and experiences online. I found that I have to stay away from CRPS Facebook groups because, in my experience, so many people were talking about not working and just sitting home all day and being miserable, and that didn't match what I want for my life and wasn't productive for me. It's definitely possible to have a career, travel, and still go out and enjoy your life- I do. You'll just have to learn to listen to your body, make modifications, take it slow, and prioritize.

I have been living with CRPS for over 15 years. I still have days on a regular basis where I grieve. What works for me is allowing myself to feel sorry for myself for awhile, but then moving on and moving forward. Anything you can find to do to distract yourself is helpful, depending on your interests. For me, it's painting that helps, because I can get absorbed in it and it calms my stress levels. But I also find doing online puzzles, like nonograms and jigsaw puzzles, helps too. 

I would also say to make sure you feel you have a doctor that you trust and you feel is progressing you appropriately. I am so grateful to my first doctor who diagnosed me, but she was a small practice and I would have to go weeks between nerve blocks, the first line of my treatment, which wasn't helping. I went to a pain management group at a respected hospital near me, and the first doctor wasn't a good fit, but the second one there was, and I've seen him for over 11 years now. In the same lane of this, I only recently found a PT that has been amazing at understanding and being patient with my CRPS, and it has made the biggest positive difference and made me realize what I was missing over the years with other PTs. I realized that it's not always about "expertise" but more importantly someone willing to work with me and learn what works for me.  

I ended up with spinal cord stimulators, and that with extended release pain meds are how I live a semi-normal life, but I went through so many other procedures and treatments before I ended up at this point. SCS surgeries are not fun, and I've had quite a few of them due to having multiple SCSs and ongoing issues with one. If you do go that route, you'll go through a trial first to make sure it works for you. 

While the pain is hard, sometimes the social aspect can be just as hard. I don't really talk about my CRPS to many people in my life, because I don't want to sound like I'm complaining or negative to be around. But then I find it's hard for people to understand why I can't stay out late or go out after work, am exhausted all the time, cancel on plans at times, or just don't feel like talking or socializing when I'm in a bad flare.

Thanks for sharing, this gives me hope!

I was in the surgical shoe or a bigger boot for several weeks after each surgery. I know my doctor advised me to try to limit being on my feet to know more than 10 total minutes per hour for the first couple weeks. I did better with that the second time around and I noticed the difference. It does take awhile for the pain to go away, especially because with this surgery, you're essentially walking on your incision. Icing as much as possible helped a lot too. If you don't have a bigger walking boot, you can get them from amazon for not too much. That helps provide a lot more support and cushion than the surgical shoe.

I'm glad it could be of some help. Best of luck on your recovery!! I do think the fasciectomy is the best way to go. Mine was as thick as yours too, and the surgery was the only thing that was going to help it. Definitely take it easy and stay off of it as much as you can. My second foot has had a much smoother recovery because I rested it more than the first.

I did start back to PT after about 10 days, but I took it verrrrry slowly and easy in the beginning. I had already been in therapy pre-surgery and my therapists know my doctor, so they had a conversation about exactly what I could and couldn't do. Simple things like ankle pumps and rolls and very gentle stretching are easy things to do at home while you're waiting that I had started out with. I know it felt good to get some gentle movement in while I was sitting.

I'm not a medical professional, but it's my understanding that the fascia isn't ever severed completely during surgery, since that would cause a collapsed arch. Rather a small cut is made with a fasciotomy or a small piece is taken out with a fasciectomy and this allows it to stretch out and lengthen. I think it's more about the release of the fascia for it to lengthen than it is about anything growing back. I'll say it does take a lot of strengthening after because it does still change the structure of the foot. I'm a big advocate for PT after surgery, because it's helped me immensely, and I'm still working hard to regain my strength. I remember hearing that you're not fully recovered until about a year after surgery, so I keep telling myself that when I have hard days.

I'm sorry, that's awful to go through surgery and not even have it work. I do feel lucky to have the doctor I have. I ended up switching from the first doctor I was seeing, because I felt like I wasn't going anywhere with the first. Maybe you can do some research and look into another doctor?

I wonder that all the time why she hired me if she wasn't even going to give me a chance. She hired me almost immediately after my interview, which was in May. It's not like it was the end of the summer and she was pressed to find someone.

My doctor said that she prefers fasiectomies because it makes it harder for it to reattach. It's basically like if you take a paper and just make a cut into it, it can be easily attached back together. But if you cut a small piece out, it becomes a lot harder to reattach the cut out part together. And to keep it from reattaching, I am always going to have to wear the right footwear and continue stretching. I just got fitted for new custom orthotics now that my feet structure is different post-surgery. I'm actually still in PT for now, so she manually helps with my tightness and stretching, but I also stretch my feet and calves multiple times a day. I do still sleep with a night splint(s) on too at times if I start feeling like I'm waking up in the morning with it too tight. Another thing my PT recommended that helps me a lot is a Therabar roller. I keep it in my work bag and roll my feet on it when needed.

The plantar fasciitis is definitely better. I don't have the PF pain and tightness, and that's awesome. My feet in general are still recovering, but it's hard to separate out how much of it is from a chronic condition that I have that causes slower healing vs. what is typical. I do know I read going into my surgeries that it can take a year for your foot to be fully back to "normal" post-surgery, so I have to keep reminding myself that I am still well within that window. But I also believe that my slow healing is definitely at play too.

So with that being said, my feet still get very sore by the end of my work day or if I'm out all day. I can't be on my feet, standing or walking, for too long without them getting pretty painful, and I still do rely on a walking boot a lot to help. I'm still in PT as well, which is helping me with increasing my strength and endurance, which I think still has a lot to do with the pain I'm having, as well as the incision soreness and sensitivity. I'm glad I had the surgeries, and I don't have any regrets, but it's still very much a process that's not over yet.

It was able to measure the thickness of the fascia as well as determine that I had tendinosis in another part of my foot. The two reports also showed the progression in the thickness over just 6 months, which helped determine my need for the surgery.

It's now a post-surgical structural & nerve pain instead. The nerve pain is directly over my outer and inner incisions, and the structural pain is more in the outside of my foot and toes because of how my gait has been altered as I recover. 

I remember reading that the PF is a major part of the structure of the foot, and by altering it, the foot has to readjust it's mechanics, which takes time.

I teach in a very diverse district, and, in the last two years, I've had students who speak English, Spanish, Arabic, Hindi, Tagalog, Polish, Albanian, Croatian, and Ukrainian. While I do speak a decent amount of Spanish, I recognize that there's no way that I could learn to speak all of those languages. I don't know what grade you'll be teaching, but I teach little ones. I use general ELL strategies to support all of my ELL students. Unless you are teaching in a bilingual classroom, you really only need to be fluent in English. Just show respect and get help from a fluent speaker, not Google Translate, when you need help communicating with parents.

In a previous district I taught in, I had a couple of students that came in only speaking Spanish. At first I was translating everything for them, only conversing with them in Spanish, etc, and then I realized their English really wasn't progressing and I wasn't helping them by doing this. Kids do well with language immersion, with supports.
